name: Esther Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead a carpentry crew repairing old shopfronts on building sites. My vocational trade certificate and years of handling settled brickwork mean I can fit new timber into an opening that isn't square, and that specialist work pays above the trade norm. I like saving a sound old facade; opening a wall to find rotten timber makes the day harder.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a transport office, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We've saved about eleven months of expenses and there are plenty of similar local building jobs. I've never used an AI tool; I use a paper site book, a tape and a probe to decide what the wall needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our shopfront crew that a faster invoice is fine, but it won't tell us whether an old lintel will carry new timber. We still need to open the wall and check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead repair work and earn above the usual carpentry rate because I can make a new frontage fit an old building. My partner's transport-office wage and eleven months of saved expenses make the mortgage and two schoolchildren comfortable in this mild picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll finish the row of shopfront repairs and keep the measured lintel notes in our site book. From each full paid month, my partner and I will make an extra mortgage payment from new wages after the children's costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I have never used an AI tool, and a shorter invoice doesn't change how I test a beam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a shop drawing miss the building?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawing showed a straight opening where the brick had settled toward the doorway. I trimmed new shopfront timber to the old wall and put its failing lintel on the repair list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra mortgage payment come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra mortgage amount would come from our next paid month, not from shifting the eleven-month reserve. If site work drops, we stop the extra payment and keep the scheduled one.

say: **Shopfront repairs** still require checking old lintels and settled walls.
**Faster invoices** do not change the carpenter's physical work.
think: My **higher trade pay** and partner's wage cover the mortgage comfortably.
An **eleven-month reserve** gives us time even if one job ends.
do: **Finish** shopfront repairs and record measured lintel conditions.
**Pay extra** mortgage principal from full paid months after children's costs.
feel: **Calm** about familiar work and secure household income.
S0.quote: I trimmed new shopfront timber to the old wall and put its failing lintel on the repair list.
fieldNote: She trusts **opened walls** and measured lintels, not a drawing alone, for repairs to old shopfronts.
Her **extra loan payments** come from future full-month wages, separately from the eleven-month reserve.

steps.text: Finish shopfront repairs and record measured lintel conditions
Pay extra mortgage principal from full paid month after children costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI will probably handle quotes, buying and bookings before robots can repair a settled shop wall. Let the office use the tool, but a carpenter must have the last word on the beam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own specialist repairs still look needed and my pay looks secure. The office might send a timber order too early, which is irritating, but we have savings and many local builders if this contractor gets careless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep photographing the opened wall and writing actual lintel sizes in the site book. If the office starts AI purchasing, I'll ask the manager to require a signed carpenter measurement before timber is cut, and I'll check the delivery against that note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a rushed order, though not frightened for our income. I prefer the site book to a new screen and don't plan to start using AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the office orders the wrong beam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the cut before the timber yard made the wrong beam and send the actual width from my tape. An old shop wall does not straighten because the office has booked a timber delivery slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a signed measurement note show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The signed note would show who opened the wall and measured the beam. I would ask the manager to keep the approval on the work order so the supplier gets one final size.

say: **AI buying** may change office work before robots repair old walls.
A **carpenter measurement** should be signed before beam timber is cut.
think: My **specialist wage** looks secure in this slower change.
A rushed **office order** would waste time, but local builders and savings give choices.
do: **Photograph** opened shop walls and record measured lintel sizes.
**Ask** manager for signed carpenter measurements before AI timber orders.
feel: **Uneasy** about ordering errors while household income stays secure.
S1.quote: An old shop wall does not straighten because the office has booked a timber delivery slot.
fieldNote: She responds to **AI purchasing** with a physical sign-off rule rather than personal tool use.
Her own **repair wage remains secure**, consistent with unease rather than income anxiety in slower change.

steps.text: Photograph opened shop walls and record measured lintel sizes
Ask manager for carpenter sign-off before any AI timber order

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 might design the shop repairs, then capable robots around 2031 might fit the timber. The builder ought to say what paid repair work stays before changing the whole site method.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 48 when the robots can work on walls. I have savings and many nearby contractors, but if our shopfront crew loses shifts, the mortgage still needs wages and the next firm may be buying the same equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the builder for a written repair rota and robot trial safety rules this month. If my paid shifts are cut, I'll apply only to posted local carpentry restoration jobs with steady hours and pay that covers the mortgage; I'll stay on this crew until I have an actual offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost repair hours, though eleven months saved and local firms give me room to choose. I won't change jobs because of a machine advert alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about a job search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner our reserve can cover a search, not a decision to work for much less forever. We would look at the mortgage amount and the children's school costs before I accepted a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What safety rules should a robot trial have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot trial would need the wall opened first, a supported lintel and a person with authority to stop the machine. I would not let a site robot remove timber above a public doorway without a supported lintel and a worker able to stop it.

say: **2028 thinking AI** designs repairs before robots fit shopfront timber around 2031.
The builder should publish **paid repair work** and safe trial rules.
think: At about **48**, robot repairs could reduce my paid shifts.
Our **eleven-month reserve** and local firms give choices, but not a permanent mortgage wage.
do: **Ask** builder for written repair rota and safe robot trial rules.
**Apply** after cuts only to posted local restoration job with steady mortgage-covering pay.
**Stay** on current paid crew until actual suitable offer exists.
feel: **Anxious** about possible shift loss, with a strong search cushion.
S2.quote: I would not let a site robot remove timber above a public doorway without a supported lintel and a worker able to stop it.
fieldNote: Her robot concern includes **lintel support** and stop authority, tied to public doorway safety.
A move requires **actual shift cuts** and posted local restoration work with steady mortgage-covering pay despite her strong reserve.

steps.text: Ask builder for written repair rota and safe robot trial rules
Apply after cuts to posted local restoration job with steady mortgage-covering pay
Stay on paid shopfront crew until suitable offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 could make the repair drawings, and robots around 2034 could do the carpentry on site. Five years gives the builder time to show which old-wall jobs a machine can really finish safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 51 at the robot date and still expect to need the shopfront wage. My savings make a course possible, but I would only take a new qualification if it kept my paid work and led to real repair posts nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the contractor about a recognised building-inspection course with fees and assessment days paid. If it provides a real place and keeps full wages during training, I'll enrol next intake; after qualifying, I will apply only if a posted local inspection job has steady hours and pay covering our mortgage and our current repair shifts have been cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible wage cut, though five years makes careful preparation possible. I still want to see a machine handle a settled wall before trusting its sales figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the inspection course have to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want practice on an actual opened wall with an instructor, then an assessment on measuring and supporting a lintel. A slide presentation about site robots would not make me a building inspector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an inspection job real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advertised job must show normal weekly hours, pay above our mortgage need and real visits to building sites. If it is only a title with a lower wage, I'll keep my current work while it is available.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes drawings before robots repair shopfronts around 2034.
Five years allows **proper safety trials** and conditional inspection training.
think: At about **51**, I may still need the higher shopfront wage.
Savings permit a course, but **full class wages** and real local posts matter.
do: **Ask** contractor for recognised inspection course with funded fees and paid assessment days.
**Enrol** if real place, fees and full class wages are secured.
**Apply** after qualification and repair cuts to posted local inspection job with steady mortgage-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible cuts, with time for a careful change.
S3.quote: A slide presentation about site robots would not make me a building inspector.
fieldNote: She ties **actual enrolment** to a funded recognised course, real place, practical assessment and full training wages.
A later application follows **qualification and repair-hour cuts**, and still requires a posted local role with dependable mortgage-covering pay.

steps.text: Ask contractor for funded inspection course and full paid assessment days
Enrol in recognised inspection course if real place, fees and full wages secured
Apply after qualification and cuts to posted local inspection job with steady mortgage-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 may draw repairs, with capable robots around 2039 doing the timber work. Ten years lets us finish many real shopfronts and show young carpenters how to test an old lintel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 56 when robots can do the hands-on repairs. The mortgage might be smaller and our children older, but I will not assume it is gone; our eleven-month reserve and local builders give us a stable near-term position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my carpentry safety certificate current and write up three old-wall repairs as examples for the younger crew. My partner and I will review the mortgage balance each year and make extra payments from future premium shifts if household costs allow, while keeping the reserve for a genuine gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our next few years, with an eye on how the trade may change later. Ten years is enough to leave clear site notes without buying a machine I do not want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a younger carpenter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a younger carpenter how to probe the timber above the door before cutting it. A tidy model cannot tell whether an old shop lintel crumbles under a screwdriver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful repair note contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first note would show the opened wall, measured beam and support we used. I'd walk the next repair with the younger fitter so the words connect to an actual building.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes drawings before robots repair timber around 2039.
A decade supports **site notes** and paid craft work while the trade evolves.
think: At about **56**, the mortgage may remain, but our current income is secure.
The **eleven-month reserve** and many local builders give room for later decisions.
do: **Keep** carpentry safety certificate current and record three old-wall repairs.
**Review** mortgage balance with partner each year.
**Pay extra** mortgage principal from future premium shifts if costs allow.
feel: **Calm** about near-term wages, watchful of distant work changes.
S4.quote: A tidy model cannot tell whether an old shop lintel crumbles under a screwdriver.
fieldNote: She remains **resistant to AI** and focuses on notes and a physical walk for younger carpenters, without claiming group action.
Her **extra mortgage payments** use future premium shift wages if affordable; held savings remain a contingency reserve.

steps.text: Keep carpentry safety certificate current and record three old-wall repairs
Review mortgage balance with partner yearly
Pay extra mortgage from future premium shifts if household costs allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because site robots around 2031 could reduce specialist shopfront shifts while we still have a mortgage. A written repair rota, safe robot trial and actual posted local work at adequate pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who carries the responsibility when a robot pulls timber from above a shop door. A shopfront can look new while the old lintel is still failing above people's heads. The finished face is not the whole repair.

headlineQuote: A shopfront can look new while the old lintel is still failing above people's heads.
portrait: **Esther**, 43, leads specialist old-shopfront carpentry with a vocational certificate, strong skill and above-average trade pay.
Her transport-office partner and two children share a **mortgage** backed by eleven months of expenses and plentiful nearby builders.
She has **never used AI**, trusts opened walls and written measurements, and prefers familiar work until change is proven.
Fast robots make her **anxious** about possible paid shifts; a decade keeps her near-term income calm while she records craft knowledge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring site robots around 2031 while specialist shopfront shifts still support the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A **written repair rota**, safe robot trial and posted local work at mortgage-covering pay would provide a fallback.
